are over 37,000 known as of 2024. A number of solar-orbiting <color=#3366CC>meteoroids</color> were large enough to be tracked in
space before striking Earth. It is now widely accepted that collisions in the past have had a significant role in
shaping the geological and biological history of Earth.
• Mars-crossing asteroids are those with perihelia above 1.3 AU which cross the orbit of Mars. As of 2024, NASA
lists 26,182 confirmed Mars-crossing asteroids.
Asteroid belt
The asteroid belt occupies a torus-shaped region between 2.3 and 3.3 AU from the Sun, which lies between the orbits
of Mars and Jupiter. It is thought to be remnants from the Solar System's formation that failed to coalesce because of
the gravitational interference of Jupiter. The asteroid belt contains tens of thousands, possibly millions, of objects over
one kilometer in diameter. Despite this, the total mass of the asteroid belt is unlikely to be more than a thousandth of
that of Earth. The asteroid belt is very sparsely populated; spacecraft routinely pass through without incident.
Below are the descriptions of the three largest bodies in the asteroid belt. They are all considered to be relatively intact
<color=#3366CC>protoplanets</color>, a precursor stage before becoming a fully-formed planet (see List of exceptional asteroids):
• Ceres (2.55–2.98 AU) is the only dwarf planet in the asteroid belt. It is the largest object in the belt, with a diameter
of 940 km. Its surface contains a mixture of <color=#3366CC>carbon</color>, frozen water and <color=#3366CC>hydrated</color> minerals. There are signs of past
cryovolcanic activity, where <color=#3366CC>volatile</color> material such as water are erupted onto the surface, as seen in surface bright
spots. Ceres has a very thin water vapor atmosphere, but practically speaking it is indistinguishable from a
vacuum.
• Pallas and Vesta (2.15–2.57 AU) is the second-largest object in the asteroid belt. Its fragments survive as the
Vesta asteroid family and numerous HED meteorites found on Earth. Vesta's surface, dominated by <color=#3366CC>basaltic</color> and
<color=#3366CC>metamorphic</color> material, has a denser composition than Ceres's. Its surface is marked by two giant craters:
Rheasilvia and Veneneia.
• <color=#3366CC>Pallas</color> (2.13–3.41 AU) is the third-largest object in the asteroid belt. It has its own Pallas asteroid family. Not much
is known about Pallas because it has never been visited by a spacecraft, though its surface is predicted to be
composed of silicates.
Hilda asteroids are in a 3:2 resonance with Jupiter; that is, they go around the Sun three times for every two Jovian
orbits. They lie in three linked clusters between Jupiter and the main asteroid belt.
<color=#3366CC>Trojans</color> are bodies located within another body's gravitationally stable <color=#3366CC>Lagrange points</color>:, 60° ahead in its orbit, or, 60°
behind in its orbit. Every planet except Mercury is known to possess at least one trojan. The <color=#3366CC>Jupiter trojan</color> population is
roughly equal to that of the asteroid belt. After Jupiter, Neptune possesses the most confirmed trojans, at 28.
Outer Solar System
The outer region of the Solar System is home to the <color=#3366CC>giant planets</color> and their large moons. The <color=#3366CC>centaurs</color> and many
<color=#3366CC>short-period comets</color> orbit in this region. Due to their greater distance from the Sun, the solid objects in the outer Solar
System contain a higher proportion of volatiles such as water, ammonia, and methane, than planets of the inner Solar
System because their lower temperatures allow these compounds to remain solid, without significant <color=#3366CC>sublimation</color>.
Outer planets
The four outer planets, called giant planets or Jovian planets, collectively make up 99% of the mass orbiting the Sun.
All four giant planets have multiple moons and a ring system, although only Saturn's rings are easily observed from
Earth. Jupiter and Saturn are composed mainly of gases with extremely low melting points, such as hydrogen, helium,
and <color=#3366CC>neon</color>, hence their designation as <color=#3366CC>gas giants</color>. Uranus and Neptune are <color=#3366CC>ice giants</color>, meaning they are largely
composed of <color=#3366CC>'ice' in the astronomical sense</color> (chemical compounds with melting points of up to a few hundred <color=#3366CC>kelvins</color>
such as water, methane, ammonia, <color=#3366CC>hydrogen sulfide</color>, and <color=#3366CC>carbon dioxide</color>.) Icy substances comprise the majority of the
satellites of the giant planets and small objects that lie beyond Neptune's orbit.
• Jupiter (4.95–5.46 AU) is the biggest and most massive planet in the Solar System. On its surface, there are
orange-brown and white cloud bands moving via the principles of <color=#3366CC>atmospheric circulation</color>, with giant storms swirling
on the surface such as the <color=#3366CC>Great Red Spot</color> and <color=#3366CC>white 'ovals'</color>. <color=#3366CC>Jupiter possesses a strong enough magnetosphere</color> to
redirect <color=#3366CC>ionizing radiation</color> and cause <color=#3366CC>auroras</color> on its poles. As of 2026, Jupiter has <color=#3366CC>115 confirmed satellites</color>, which
can roughly be sorted into three groups:
• The Amalthea group, consisting of Metis, Adrastea, Amalthea, and Thebe. They orbit substantially closer to Jupiter
than other satellites. Materials from these natural satellites are the source of Jupiter's faint ring.

• The <color=#3366CC>Galilean moons</color>, consisting of <color=#3366CC>Ganymede</color>, <color=#3366CC>Callisto</color>, <color=#3366CC>Io</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Europa</color>. They are the largest moons of Jupiter and
exhibit planetary properties.
• Irregular satellites, consisting of substantially smaller natural satellites. They have more distant orbits than the other
objects.
• Saturn (9.08–10.12 AU) has a distinctive visible <color=#3366CC>ring system</color> orbiting around its equator composed of small ice and
rock particles. Like Jupiter, it is mostly made of hydrogen and helium. At its north and south poles, Saturn has
peculiar <color=#3366CC>hexagon-shaped storms</color> larger than the diameter of Earth. <color=#3366CC>Saturn has a magnetosphere</color> capable of
producing weak auroras. As of 2026, Saturn has <color=#3366CC>293 confirmed satellites</color>, grouped into:
• Ring moonlets and shepherds, which orbit inside or close to Saturn's rings. A moonlet can only partially clear out
dust in its orbit, while the ring shepherds are able to completely clear out dust, forming visible gaps in the rings.

• Inner large satellites <color=#3366CC>Mimas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Enceladus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tethys</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Dione</color>. These satellites orbit within <color=#3366CC>Saturn's E ring</color>. They are
composed mostly of water ice and are believed to have differentiated internal structures.
• Trojan moons Calypso and Telesto (trojans of Tethys), and Helene and Polydeuces (trojans of Dione). These small
moons share their orbits with Tethys and Dione, leading or trailing either.
• Outer large satellites <color=#3366CC>Rhea</color>, <color=#3366CC>Titan</color>, Hyperion, and <color=#3366CC>Iapetus</color>. Titan is the only satellite in the Solar System to have a
substantial atmosphere.
• Irregular satellites, consisting of substantially smaller natural satellites. They have more distant orbits than the other
objects. Phoebe is the largest irregular satellite of Saturn.
• Uranus (18.3–20.1 AU), uniquely among the planets, orbits the Sun on its side with an <color=#3366CC>axial tilt</color> ›90°. This gives the
planet extreme seasonal variation as each pole points alternately toward and then away from the Sun. Uranus's
outer layer has a muted <color=#3366CC>cyan</color> color, but underneath these clouds are many mysteries about its climate, such as
unusually low internal heat and erratic cloud formation. As of 2026, Uranus has <color=#3366CC>29 confirmed satellites</color>, divided into
three groups:
• Inner satellites, which orbit inside Uranus's ring system. They are very close to each other, which suggests that
their orbits are <color=#3366CC>chaotic</color>.

• Large satellites, consisting of <color=#3366CC>Titania</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oberon</color>, <color=#3366CC>Umbriel</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ariel</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Miranda</color>. Most of them have roughly equal
amounts of rock and ice, except Miranda, which is made primarily of ice.
• Irregular satellites, having more distant and eccentric orbits than the other objects.
• Neptune (29.9–30.5 AU) is the furthest planet known in the Solar System. Its outer atmosphere has a slightly
muted cyan color, with occasional storms on the surface that look like dark spots. Like Uranus, many atmospheric
phenomena of Neptune are unexplained, such as the <color=#3366CC>thermosphere</color>'s abnormally high temperature or the strong tilt
(47°) of its magnetosphere. As of 2026, Neptune has <color=#3366CC>16 confirmed satellites</color>, divided into two groups:
• Regular satellites, which have circular orbits that lie near Neptune's equator.
• Irregular satellites, which as the name implies, have less regular orbits. One of them, <color=#3366CC>Triton</color>, is Neptune's largest
moon. It is geologically active, with erupting <color=#3366CC>geysers</color> of nitrogen gas, and possesses a thin, cloudy nitrogen
atmosphere.
Centaurs
The centaurs are icy, comet-like bodies whose semi-major axes are longer than Jupiter's and shorter than Neptune's
(between 5.5 and 30 AU). These are former Kuiper belt and <color=#3366CC>scattered disc objects</color> (SDOs) that were gravitationally
perturbed closer to the Sun by the outer planets, and are expected to become comets or be ejected out of the Solar
System. While most centaurs are inactive and asteroid-like, some exhibit cometary activity, such as the first centaur
discovered, <color=#3366CC>2060 Chiron</color>, which has been classified as a comet (95P) because it develops a coma just as comets do
when they approach the Sun. The largest known centaur, 10199 Chariklo, has a diameter of about 250 km and is one
of the few minor planets possessing a ring system.
Trans-Neptunian region
Beyond the orbit of Neptune lies the area of the "<color=#3366CC>trans-Neptunian region</color>", with the doughnut-shaped Kuiper belt, home
of Pluto and several other dwarf planets, and an overlapping disc of scattered objects, which is <color=#3366CC>tilted toward the plane</color>
of the Solar System and reaches much further out than the Kuiper belt. The entire region is still largely unexplored. It
appears to consist overwhelmingly of many thousands of small worlds – the largest having a diameter only a fifth that of
Earth and a mass far smaller than that of the Moon – composed mainly of rock and ice. This region is sometimes
described as the "third zone of the Solar System", enclosing the inner and the outer Solar System.
Kuiper belt
The Kuiper belt is a great ring of debris similar to the asteroid belt, but consisting mainly of objects composed primarily
of ice. It extends between 30 and 50 AU from the Sun. It is composed mainly of small Solar System bodies, although
the largest few are probably large enough to be dwarf planets. There are estimated to be over 100,000 Kuiper belt
objects with a diameter greater than 50 km, but the total mass of the Kuiper belt is thought to be only a tenth or even a
hundredth the mass of Earth. Many Kuiper belt objects have satellites, and most have orbits that are substantially
inclined (~10°) to the plane of the ecliptic.
The Kuiper belt can be roughly divided into the "classical" belt and the resonant trans-Neptunian objects. The latter
have orbits whose periods are in a simple ratio to that of Neptune: for example, going around the Sun twice for every
three times that Neptune does, or once for every two. The classical belt consists of objects having no resonance with
Neptune, and extends from roughly 39.4 to 47.7 AU. Members of the classical Kuiper belt are sometimes called
"cubewanos", after the first of their kind to be discovered, originally designated 1992 QB1, (and has since been named
Albion); they are still in near primordial, low-eccentricity orbits.
There is strong consensus among astronomers that five members of the Kuiper belt are Others. Many dwarf planet
candidates are being considered, pending further data for verification.
• Pluto and Charon (29.7–49.3 AU) is the largest known object in the Kuiper belt. Pluto has a relatively eccentric
orbit, inclined 17 degrees to the <color=#3366CC>ecliptic plane</color>. Pluto has a <color=#3366CC>2:3 resonance</color> with Neptune, meaning that Pluto orbits
twice around the Sun for every three Neptunian orbits. Kuiper belt objects whose orbits share this resonance are
called plutinos. <color=#3366CC>Pluto has five moons</color>: Charon, Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra.
• <color=#3366CC>Charon</color>, the largest of Pluto's moons, is sometimes described as part of a binary system with Pluto, as the two
bodies orbit a <color=#3366CC>barycenter</color> of gravity above their surfaces (i.e. they appear to "orbit each other").
• (30.3–48.1 AU), is in the same 2:3 orbital resonance with Neptune as Pluto, and is the largest such object after
Pluto itself. Its eccentricity and inclination are similar to Pluto's, but its perihelion lies about 120° from that of Pluto.
Thus, the <color=#3366CC>phase</color> of Orcus's orbit is opposite to Pluto's: Orcus is at aphelion (most recently in 2019) around when
Pluto is at perihelion (most recently in 1989) and vice versa. For this reason, it has been called the anti-Pluto. It has
one known moon, Vanth.
• <color=#3366CC>Haumea</color> (34.6–51.6 AU) was discovered in 2005. It is in a temporary 7:12 orbital resonance with Neptune. Haumea
possesses a ring system, two known moons named Hiiaka and Namaka, and rotates so quickly (once every 3.9
hours) that it is stretched into an ellipsoid. It is part of a collisional family of Kuiper belt objects that share similar
orbits, which suggests a giant impact on Haumea ejected fragments into space billions of years ago.
• <color=#3366CC>Makemake</color> (38.1–52.8 AU), although smaller than Pluto, is the largest known object in the classical Kuiper belt
(that is, a Kuiper belt object not in a confirmed resonance with Neptune). Makemake is the brightest object in the
Kuiper belt after Pluto. Discovered in 2005, it was officially named in 2008. Its orbit is far more inclined than Pluto's,
at 29°. It has one known moon, S/2015 (136472) 1.
• (41.9–45.5 AU) is the second-largest known object in the classical Kuiper belt, after Makemake. Its orbit is
significantly less eccentric and inclined than those of Makemake or Haumea. It possesses a ring system and one
known moon, Weywot.
Scattered disc
The scattered disc, which overlaps the Kuiper belt but extends out to near 500 AU, is thought to be the source of
short-period comets. Scattered-disc objects are believed to have been perturbed into erratic orbits by the gravitational
influence of <color=#3366CC>Neptune's early outward migration</color>. Most scattered disc objects have perihelia within the Kuiper belt but
aphelia far beyond it (some more than 150 AU from the Sun). SDOs' orbits can be inclined up to 46.8° from the ecliptic
plane. Some astronomers consider the scattered disc to be merely another region of the Kuiper belt and describe
scattered-disc objects as "scattered Kuiper belt objects". Some astronomers classify centaurs as inward-scattered
Kuiper belt objects along with the outward-scattered residents of the scattered disc.
Currently, there is strong consensus among astronomers that two of the bodies in the scattered disc are Gonggong and
Eris:
• (38.3–97.5 AU) is the largest known scattered disc object and the most massive known dwarf planet. Eris's
discovery contributed to a debate about the definition of a planet because it is 25% more massive than Pluto and
about the same diameter. It has one known moon, <color=#3366CC>Dysnomia</color>. Like Pluto, its orbit is highly eccentric, with a
perihelion of 38.2 AU (roughly Pluto's distance from the Sun) and an aphelion of 97.6 AU, and steeply inclined to
the ecliptic plane at an angle of 44°.
• (33.8–101.2 AU) is a dwarf planet in a comparable orbit to Eris, except that it is in a 3:10 resonance with Neptune.
It has one known moon, Xiangliu.
Extreme trans-Neptunian objects
Some objects in the Solar System have a very large orbit, and therefore are much less affected by the known giant
planets than other minor planet populations. These bodies are called extreme trans-Neptunian objects, or ETNOs for
short. Generally, ETNOs' semi-major axes are at least 150–250 AU wide. For example, 541132 Leleākūhonua orbits
the Sun once every ~32,000 years, with a distance of 65–2000 AU from the Sun.
This population is divided into three subgroups by astronomers. The <color=#3366CC>scattered</color> ETNOs have <color=#3366CC>perihelia</color> around 38–45 AU
and an exceptionally high <color=#3366CC>eccentricity</color> of more than 0.85. As with the regular scattered disc objects, they were likely
formed as result of gravitational scattering by Neptune and still interact with the giant planets. The detached ETNOs,
with perihelia approximately between 40–45 and 50–60 AU, are less affected by Neptune than the scattered ETNOs,
but are still relatively close to Neptune. The <color=#3366CC>sednoids</color> or <color=#3366CC>inner Oort cloud</color> objects, with perihelia beyond 50–60 AU, are
too far from Neptune to be strongly influenced by it.
Currently, there is one ETNO that is classified as a dwarf planet:
• (76.2–937 AU) was the first extreme trans-Neptunian object to be discovered. It is a large, reddish object, and
takes ~11,400 years to complete one orbit. <color=#3366CC>Mike Brown</color>, who discovered the object in 2003, asserts that it cannot
be part of the scattered disc or the Kuiper belt because its perihelion is too distant to have been affected by
Neptune's migration. The <color=#3366CC>sednoid population</color> is named after Sedna.
Statistical variance has been observed in the orbits of some extreme trans-Neptunian objects, whose closest
approaches to the Sun are mostly clustered around one sector and who display a similar orbital tilt to each other. Some
astronomers have suggested that this may be the result of the influence of a large planet beyond Neptune; this
hypothetical planet has been termed <color=#3366CC>Planet Nine</color>. Others credit this statistical variance to observational biases or sheer
<color=#3366CC>coincidence</color>.
Oort cloud
The <color=#3366CC>Oort cloud</color> is a theorized spherical shell of up to a trillion icy objects that is thought to be the source for all
long-period comets, which were originally ejected from the planetary region by gravitational interactions with the gas
giants. Oort cloud objects move very slowly, and can be perturbed by infrequent events, such as collisions, the
gravitational effects of a passing star, or the <color=#3366CC>galactic tide</color>, the <color=#3366CC>tidal force</color> exerted by the Milky Way. No direct
observation of the Oort cloud is possible with present imaging technology. The probe that is currently nearest to the
Oort cloud, <color=#3366CC>Voyager 1</color>, is expected to reach it in 300 years.
The Oort cloud is theorized to surround the Solar System from potentially ~2,000 AU from the Sun to up to ~200,000
AU. Lower estimates for the radius of the Oort cloud, by contrast, do not place it farther than 50,000 AU. Most of the
mass is orbiting in the region between 3,000 and 100,000 AU. The furthest known objects, such as Comet West, have
aphelia around 70,000 AU from the Sun.
Gravitationally unstable populations
Meteoroids, meteors and dust
Solid objects smaller than one meter are usually called meteoroids and micrometeoroids (grain-sized), with the exact
division between the two categories being debated over the years. By 2017, the IAU designated any solid object having
a diameter between ~30 micrometers and 1 meter as meteoroids, and depreciated the micrometeoroid categorization,
instead terms smaller particles simply as 'dust particles'.
Some meteoroids formed via disintegration of comets and asteroids, while a few formed via impact debris ejected from
planetary bodies. Most meteoroids are made of silicates and heavier metals like <color=#3366CC>nickel</color> and <color=#3366CC>iron</color>. When passing through
the Solar System, comets produce a trail of meteoroids; it is hypothesized that this is caused either by vaporization of
the comet's material or by simple breakup of dormant comets. When crossing an atmosphere, these meteoroids will
produce bright streaks in the sky due to atmospheric entry, called <color=#3366CC>meteors</color>. If a stream of meteoroids enter the
atmosphere on parallel trajectories, the meteors will seemingly 'radiate' from a point in the sky, hence the
phenomenon's name: <color=#3366CC>meteor shower</color>.
The inner Solar System is home to the <color=#3366CC>zodiacal dust cloud</color>, which is visible as the hazy <color=#3366CC>zodiacal light</color> in dark,
unpolluted skies. It may be generated by collisions within the asteroid belt brought on by gravitational interactions with
the planets; a more recent proposed origin is materials from planet Mars. The outer Solar System hosts a cosmic dust
cloud. It extends from about 10 AU to about 40 AU, and was probably created by collisions within the Kuiper belt.
Comets
Comets are small Solar System bodies, typically only a few kilometers across, composed largely of volatile ices. They
have highly eccentric orbits, generally a perihelion within the orbits of the inner planets and an aphelion far beyond
Pluto. When a comet enters the inner Solar System, its proximity to the Sun causes its icy surface to <color=#3366CC>sublimate</color> and
<color=#3366CC>ionise</color>, creating a coma: a long tail of gas and dust often visible to the naked eye.
Short-period comets have orbits lasting less than two hundred years. Long-period comets have orbits lasting thousands
of years. Short-period comets are thought to originate in the Kuiper belt, whereas long-period comets, such as
<color=#3366CC>Hale–Bopp</color>, are thought to originate in the Oort cloud. Many comet groups, such as the <color=#3366CC>Kreutz sungrazers</color>, formed from
the breakup of a single parent. Some comets with hyperbolic orbits may originate outside the Solar System, but
determining their precise orbits is difficult. Old comets whose volatiles have mostly been driven out by solar warming
are often categorized as asteroids.
Boundary region and uncertainties
Much of the outer reaches of the Solar System is still unknown. The region beyond 100 AU away is virtually unexplored
and learning about this region of space is difficult. Study of this region depends upon inferences from those few objects
whose orbits happen to be perturbed such that they fall closer to the Sun, and even then, detecting these objects has
often been possible only when they happened to become bright enough to register as comets. Many objects are yet to
be discovered in the Solar System's outer region.
The Sun's Hill sphere, its <color=#3366CC>gravitational potential</color> reaching the galactic potential, the potential of the galactic nucleus, the
effective range of its gravitational influence, is thought to encompass the Oort cloud, and extend to up to 230,000 AU
from the Sun.
The boundaries of the <color=#3366CC>heliosphere</color> and of the Hill sphere, the Sun's gravitational potential in respect to the <color=#3366CC>interstellar</color>
<color=#3366CC>medium</color> and the galactic gravitational potential, at the edge of the <color=#3366CC>Oort cloud</color>, represent the boundaries of the Solar
System with the galactic environment it is in.
Edge of the heliosphere
The Sun's stellar-wind bubble, the <color=#3366CC>heliosphere</color>, a region of space dominated by the Sun, has its boundary at the
termination shock. Based on the Sun's peculiar motion relative to the local standard of rest, this boundary is roughly
80–100 AU from the Sun upwind of the interstellar medium and roughly 200 AU from the Sun downwind. Here the solar
wind collides with the interstellar medium and dramatically slows, condenses and becomes more turbulent, forming a
great oval structure known as the <color=#3366CC>heliosheath</color>.
The heliosheath has been theorized to look and behave very much like a comet's tail, extending outward for a further
40 AU on the upwind side but tailing many times that distance downwind to possibly several thousands of AU.
Evidence from the <color=#3366CC>Cassini</color> and Interstellar Boundary Explorer spacecraft has suggested that it is forced into a bubble
shape by the constraining action of the interstellar magnetic field, but the actual shape remains unknown.
The shape and form of the outer edge of the heliosphere is likely affected by the <color=#3366CC>fluid dynamics</color> of interactions with the
interstellar medium as well as <color=#3366CC>solar magnetic fields</color> prevailing to the south, e.g. it is bluntly shaped with the northern
hemisphere extending 9 AU farther than the southern hemisphere. The heliopause is considered the beginning of the
interstellar medium. Beyond the heliopause, at around 230 AU, lies the bow shock: a plasma "wake" left by the Sun as
it travels through the Milky Way. Large objects outside the heliopause remain gravitationally bound to the Sun, but the
flow of matter in the interstellar medium homogenizes the distribution of micro-scale objects.
Celestial neighborhood
Within 10 light-years of the Sun there are relatively few stars, the closest being the triple star system <color=#3366CC>Alpha Centauri</color>,
which is about 4.4 light-years away and may be in the Local Bubble's <color=#3366CC>G-Cloud</color>. Alpha Centauri A and B are a closely
tied pair of Sun-like stars, whereas the closest star to the Sun, the small <color=#3366CC>red dwarf</color> <color=#3366CC>Proxima Centauri</color>, orbits the pair at a
distance of 0.2 light-years. In 2016, a potentially habitable <color=#3366CC>exoplanet</color> was found to be orbiting Proxima Centauri, called
<color=#3366CC>Proxima Centauri b</color>, the closest confirmed exoplanet to the Sun.
The Solar System is surrounded by the <color=#3366CC>Local Interstellar Cloud</color>, although it is not clear if it is embedded in the Local
Interstellar Cloud or if it lies just outside the cloud's edge. Multiple other <color=#3366CC>interstellar clouds</color> exist in the region within 300
light-years of the Sun, known as the <color=#3366CC>Local Bubble</color>. The latter feature is an hourglass-shaped cavity or <color=#3366CC>superbubble</color> in
the interstellar medium roughly 300 light-years across. The bubble is suffused with high-temperature plasma,
suggesting that it may be the product of several recent supernovae.
The Local Bubble is a small superbubble compared to the neighboring wider Radcliffe Wave and Split linear structures
(formerly Gould Belt), each of which are some thousands of light-years in length. All these structures are part of the
<color=#3366CC>Orion Arm</color>, which contains most of the stars in the Milky Way that are visible to the unaided eye.
Groups of stars form together in <color=#3366CC>star clusters</color>, before dissolving into co-moving associations. A prominent grouping that
is visible to the naked eye is the Ursa Major moving group, which is around 80 light-years away within the Local
Bubble. The nearest star cluster is <color=#3366CC>Hyades</color>, which lies at the edge of the Local Bubble. The closest star-forming regions
are the Corona Australis Molecular Cloud, the <color=#3366CC>Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex</color> and the Taurus molecular cloud; the latter
lies just beyond the Local Bubble and is part of the Radcliffe wave.
Stellar flybys that pass within 0.25 pc of the Sun occur roughly once every 100,000 years. The closest well-measured
approach was Scholz's Star, which approached to ~50,000 AU of the Sun some ~70 thousand years ago, likely passing
through the outer Oort cloud. There is a 1% chance every billion years that a star will pass within 100 AU of the Sun,
potentially disrupting the Solar System.
Galactic position
The Solar System is located in the <color=#3366CC>Milky Way</color>, a <color=#3366CC>barred spiral galaxy</color> with a diameter of about 100,000 <color=#3366CC>light-years</color>
containing more than 100 billion stars. The Sun is part of one of the Milky Way's outer spiral arms, known as the
<color=#3366CC>Orion–Cygnus Arm</color> or Local Spur. It is a member of the <color=#3366CC>thin disk</color> population of stars orbiting close to the galactic plane.
Its speed around the center of the Milky Way is about 220 km/s, so that it completes one revolution every 240 million
years. This revolution is known as the Solar System's galactic year. The solar apex, the direction of the Sun's path
through interstellar space, is near the constellation <color=#3366CC>Hercules</color> in the direction of the current location of the bright star
<color=#3366CC>Vega</color>. The plane of the ecliptic lies at an angle of about 60° to the <color=#3366CC>galactic plane</color>.
The Sun follows a nearly circular orbit around the <color=#3366CC>Galactic Center</color> (where the <color=#3366CC>supermassive black hole</color> <color=#3366CC>Sagittarius A*</color>
resides) at a distance of 26,660 light-years, orbiting at roughly the same speed as that of the spiral arms. If it orbited
close to the center, gravitational tugs from nearby stars could perturb bodies in the Oort cloud and send many comets
into the inner Solar System, producing collisions with potentially catastrophic implications for life on Earth. In this
scenario, the intense radiation of the Galactic Center could interfere with the development of complex life.
The Solar System's location in the Milky Way is a factor in the <color=#3366CC>evolutionary history of life</color> on Earth. Spiral arms are
home to a far larger concentration of <color=#3366CC>supernovae</color>, gravitational instabilities, and radiation that could disrupt the Solar
System, but since Earth stays in the Local Spur and therefore does not pass frequently through spiral arms, this has
given Earth long periods of stability for life to evolve. However, according to the controversial Shiva hypothesis, the
changing position of the Solar System relative to other parts of the Milky Way could explain periodic <color=#3366CC>extinction events</color>
on Earth.
Discovery and exploration
Humanity's knowledge of the Solar System has grown incrementally over the centuries. Although the <color=#3366CC>ancient Greek</color>
philosopher <color=#3366CC>Aristarchus of Samos</color> had speculated on a <color=#3366CC>heliocentric</color> reordering of the cosmos, up to the <color=#3366CC>Late Middle</color>
<color=#3366CC>Ages</color>–<color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>, astronomers from Europe to India believed Earth to <color=#3366CC>be stationary at the center</color> of the universe and
categorically different from the divine or ethereal objects that moved through the sky. <color=#3366CC>Nicolaus Copernicus</color> was the first
person known to have developed a mathematically predictive heliocentric system.
Heliocentrism did not triumph immediately over geocentrism, but the work of Copernicus had its champions, notably
<color=#3366CC>Johannes Kepler</color>. Using a heliocentric model that improved upon Copernicus by allowing orbits to be elliptical, and the
precise observational data of <color=#3366CC>Tycho Brahe</color>, Kepler produced the Rudolphine Tables, which enabled accurate
computations of the positions of the then-known planets. Pierre Gassendi used them to predict a <color=#3366CC>transit of Mercury</color> in
1631, and Jeremiah Horrocks did the same for a <color=#3366CC>transit of Venus</color> in 1639. This provided a strong vindication of
heliocentrism and Kepler's elliptical orbits.
In the 17th century, <color=#3366CC>Galileo</color> publicized the use of the telescope in astronomy; he and Simon Marius independently
discovered that Jupiter had four satellites in orbit around it. <color=#3366CC>Christiaan Huygens</color> followed on from these observations by
discovering Saturn's moon <color=#3366CC>Titan</color> and the shape of the <color=#3366CC>rings of Saturn</color>. In 1677, <color=#3366CC>Edmond Halley</color> observed a transit of
Mercury across the Sun, leading him to realize that observations of the solar parallax of a planet (more ideally using the
transit of Venus) could be used to <color=#3366CC>trigonometrically</color> determine the distances between Earth, <color=#3366CC>Venus</color>, and the Sun.
Halley's friend <color=#3366CC>Isaac Newton</color>, in his magisterial <color=#3366CC>Principia Mathematica</color> of 1687, demonstrated that celestial bodies are
not quintessentially different from Earthly ones: the same <color=#3366CC>laws of motion</color> and of <color=#3366CC>gravity</color> apply on Earth and in the skies.
The term "Solar System" entered the English language by 1704, when <color=#3366CC>John Locke</color> used it to refer to the Sun, planets,
and comets. In 1705, Halley realized that repeated sightings of <color=#3366CC>a comet</color> were of the same object, returning regularly
once every 75–76 years. This was the first evidence that anything other than the planets repeatedly orbited the Sun,
though <color=#3366CC>Seneca</color> had theorized this about comets in the 1st century. Careful observations of the 1769 transit of Venus
allowed astronomers to calculate the average Earth–Sun distance as 93726900 mi, only 0.8% greater than the modern
value.
<color=#3366CC>Uranus</color>, having occasionally been observed since 1690 and possibly from antiquity, was recognized to be a planet
orbiting beyond Saturn by 1783. In 1838, <color=#3366CC>Friedrich Bessel</color> successfully measured a <color=#3366CC>stellar parallax</color>, an apparent shift in
the position of a star created by Earth's motion around the Sun, providing the first direct, experimental proof of
heliocentrism. <color=#3366CC>Neptune</color> was identified as a planet some years later, in 1846, thanks to its gravitational pull causing a
slight but detectable variation in the orbit of Uranus. <color=#3366CC>Mercury's orbital anomaly</color> observations led to searches for Vulcan,
a planet interior of Mercury, but these attempts were quashed with <color=#3366CC>Albert Einstein</color>'s theory of <color=#3366CC>general relativity</color> in 1915.
In the 20th century, humans began their space exploration around the Solar System, starting with placing <color=#3366CC>telescopes in</color>
<color=#3366CC>space</color> since the 1960s. By 1989, all eight planets have been visited by space probes. Probes have returned samples
from comets and asteroids, as well as flown through the <color=#3366CC>Sun's corona</color> and visited two dwarf planets (<color=#3366CC>Pluto</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ceres</color>).
To save on fuel, some space missions make use of <color=#3366CC>gravity assist maneuvers</color>, such as the two <color=#3366CC>Voyager probes</color>
accelerating when flying by planets in the outer Solar System and the Parker Solar Probe decelerating closer towards
the Sun after its flyby of Venus.
Humans have landed on the Moon during the <color=#3366CC>Apollo program</color> in the 1960s and 1970s and are planning to return to the
Moon in the 2020s with the Artemis program. Discoveries in the 20th and 21st century has prompted the <color=#3366CC>redefinition of</color>
<color=#3366CC>the term planet</color> in 2006, hence the reclassification of Pluto as a dwarf planet, and further interest in <color=#3366CC>trans-Neptunian</color>
<color=#3366CC>objects</color>.
Computer

A computer is a <color=#3366CC>machine</color> that can be <color=#3366CC>programmed</color> to automatically <color=#3366CC>carry out</color> sequences of <color=#3366CC>arithmetic</color> or <color=#3366CC>logical</color>
<color=#3366CC>operations</color> (<color=#3366CC>computation</color>). Modern <color=#3366CC>digital electronic</color> computers can perform generic sets of operations known as
<color=#3366CC>programs</color>, which enable computers to perform a wide range of tasks. The term computer system may refer to a
nominally complete computer that includes the <color=#3366CC>hardware</color>, <color=#3366CC>operating system</color>, <color=#3366CC>software</color>, and peripheral equipment
needed and used for full operation, or to a group of computers that are linked and function together, such as a
<color=#3366CC>computer network</color> or <color=#3366CC>computer cluster</color>.
Numbering only a few in the 1930s, today computers are ubiquitous over a broad range of industrial and <color=#3366CC>consumer</color>
<color=#3366CC>products</color> that use computers as control systems. The price, size, and complexity of computers can range from simple

<color=#3366CC>single-purpose devices</color> like key fobs, <color=#3366CC>microwave ovens</color>, and <color=#3366CC>remote controls</color> up to <color=#3366CC>supercomputers</color> and factories using
<color=#3366CC>industrial robots</color>. Computers are at the core of general-purpose devices such as <color=#3366CC>personal computers</color> and <color=#3366CC>mobile</color>
<color=#3366CC>devices</color>, such as <color=#3366CC>smartphones</color>. Computers power the <color=#3366CC>Internet</color>, which links billions of computers and users.
Early computers were meant to be used only for calculations. Simple manual instruments like the <color=#3366CC>abacus</color> have aided
people in doing calculations since ancient times. Early in the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>, some mechanical devices were built
to automate long, tedious tasks, such as guiding patterns for <color=#3366CC>looms</color>. More sophisticated electrical machines did
specialized <color=#3366CC>analog</color> calculations in the early 20th century. Early <color=#3366CC>digital</color> electronic calculating machines were developed

during <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, beginning with electromechanicals (1930s), <color=#3366CC>thermionic valves</color> (1930s), <color=#3366CC>semiconductor</color> <color=#3366CC>transistors</color>
(1940s), <color=#3366CC>MOSFET</color> (MOS transistors 1950s), and finally <color=#3366CC>monolithic integrated circuits</color> (1950s+). With each technology
advancement resulting in smaller, more efficient circuit designs that lead to the <color=#3366CC>microprocessor</color> and the microcomputer
revolution in the 1970s. Since then the speed, computing power, and versatility of computers have been increasing
dramatically with transistor counts increasing at a rapid pace (<color=#3366CC>Moore's law</color> noted that counts doubled every two years),
leading to the <color=#3366CC>Digital Revolution</color> during the late 20th and early 21st centuries.
Conventionally, a modern computer consists of at least one processing element, typically a <color=#3366CC>central processing unit</color>
(CPU) in the form of a <color=#3366CC>microprocessor</color>, together with some type of <color=#3366CC>computer memory</color>, typically semiconductor memory
chips. The processing element carries out arithmetic and logical operations, and a sequencing and control unit can
change the order of operations in response to stored <color=#3366CC>information</color>. Peripheral devices include input devices (keyboards,

<color=#3366CC>mice</color>, joysticks, etc.), output devices (<color=#3366CC>monitors</color>, <color=#3366CC>printers</color>, etc.), and <color=#3366CC>input/output devices</color> that perform both functions (e.g.
<color=#3366CC>touchscreens</color>). Peripheral devices allow information to be retrieved from an external source, and they enable the
results of operations to be saved and retrieved.
Etymology
It was not until the mid-20th century that the word acquired its modern definition; according to the <color=#3366CC>Oxford English</color>
<color=#3366CC>Dictionary</color>, the first known use of the word computer was in a different sense, in a 1613 book called The Yong Mans
Gleanings by the English writer Richard Brathwait: "I haue read the truest computer of Times, and the best
Arithmetician that euer breathed, and he reduceth thy dayes into a short number." This usage of the term referred to a
human computer, a person who carried out calculations or <color=#3366CC>computations</color>. The word continued to have the same
meaning until the middle of the 20th century. During the latter part of this period, women were often hired as computers
because they could be paid less than their male counterparts. By 1943, most human computers were women.
The Online Etymology Dictionary gives the first attested use of computer in the 1640s, meaning 'one who calculates';
this is an "agent noun from compute (v.)". The Online Etymology Dictionary states that the use of the term to mean
calculating machine' (of any type) is from 1897." The Online Etymology Dictionary indicates that the "modern use" of
the term, to mean 'programmable digital electronic computer' dates from "1945 under this name; [in a] theoretical
[sense] from 1937, as <color=#3366CC>Turing machine</color>". The name has remained, although modern computers are capable of many
higher-level functions.
History
Pre-20th century
Devices have been used to aid computation for thousands of years, mostly using <color=#3366CC>one-to-one correspondence</color> with
fingers. The earliest counting device was most likely a form of tally stick. Later record keeping aids throughout the
<color=#3366CC>Fertile Crescent</color> included calculi (clay spheres, cones, etc.) which represented counts of items, likely livestock or grains,
sealed in hollow unbaked clay containers. The use of counting rods is one example.
The <color=#3366CC>abacus</color> was initially used for arithmetic tasks. The Roman abacus was developed from devices used in <color=#3366CC>Babylonia</color>
as early as 2400 BCE. Since then, many other forms of reckoning boards or tables have been invented. In a medieval
European counting house, a checkered cloth would be placed on a table, and markers moved around on it according to
certain rules, as an aid to calculating sums of money.
The <color=#3366CC>Antikythera mechanism</color> is believed to be the earliest known mechanical <color=#3366CC>analog computer</color>, according to Derek J. de
Solla Price. It was designed to calculate astronomical positions. It was discovered in 1901 in the Antikythera wreck off
the Greek island of Antikythera, between Kythera and <color=#3366CC>Crete</color>, and has been dated to approximately c. 100 BCE.
Devices of comparable complexity to the Antikythera mechanism would not reappear until the fourteenth century.
Many mechanical aids to calculation and measurement were constructed for astronomical and navigation use. The
planisphere was a <color=#3366CC>star chart</color> invented by <color=#3366CC>Abū Rayhān al-Bīrūnī</color> in the early 11th century. The <color=#3366CC>astrolabe</color> was invented in
the <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic world</color> in either the 1st or 2nd centuries BCE and is often attributed to <color=#3366CC>Hipparchus</color>. A combination of the
planisphere and dioptra, the astrolabe was effectively an analog computer capable of working out several different
kinds of problems in <color=#3366CC>spherical astronomy</color>. An astrolabe incorporating a mechanical <color=#3366CC>calendar</color> computer and <color=#3366CC>gear</color>-wheels
was invented by Abi Bakr of <color=#3366CC>Isfahan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Persia</color> in 1235. Abū Rayhān al-Bīrūnī invented the first mechanical geared
<color=#3366CC>lunisolar calendar</color> astrolabe, an early fixed-<color=#3366CC>wired</color> knowledge processing machine with a gear train and gear-wheels, c.
The sector, a calculating instrument used for solving problems in proportion, <color=#3366CC>trigonometry</color>, multiplication and division,
and for various functions, such as squares and cube roots, was developed in the late 16th century and found
application in gunnery, surveying, and navigation.
The planimeter was a manual instrument to calculate the area of a closed figure by tracing over it with a mechanical
linkage.
The <color=#3366CC>slide rule</color> was invented around 1620–1630 by the English clergyman <color=#3366CC>William Oughtred</color>, shortly after the publication
of the concept of the <color=#3366CC>logarithm</color>. It is a hand-operated analog computer for doing multiplication and division. As slide rule
development progressed, added scales provided reciprocals, squares and square roots, cubes and cube roots, as well
as transcendental functions such as logarithms and exponentials, circular and <color=#3366CC>hyperbolic</color> trigonometry, and other
<color=#3366CC>functions</color>. Slide rules with special scales are still used for quick performance of routine calculations, such as the E6B
circular slide rule used for time and distance calculations on light aircraft.
In the 1770s, Pierre Jaquet-Droz, a Swiss <color=#3366CC>watchmaker</color>, built a mechanical doll (<color=#3366CC>automaton</color>) that could write holding a
quill pen. By switching the number and order of its internal wheels, different letters, and hence different messages,
could be produced. In effect, it could be mechanically "programmed" to read instructions. Along with two other complex
machines, the doll is at the Musée d'Art et d'Histoire of Neuchâtel, <color=#3366CC>Switzerland</color>, and still operates.
In 1831–1835, mathematician and engineer Giovanni Plana devised a Perpetual Calendar machine, which through a
system of pulleys and cylinders could predict the perpetual calendar for every year from 0 CE (that is, 1 BCE) to 4000
CE, keeping track of leap years and varying day length. The tide-predicting machine invented by the Scottish scientist
<color=#3366CC>Sir William Thomson</color> in 1872 was of great utility to navigation in shallow waters. It used a system of pulleys and wires to
automatically calculate predicted tide levels for a set period at a particular location.
The differential analyser, a mechanical analog computer designed to solve <color=#3366CC>differential equations</color> by <color=#3366CC>integration</color>, used
wheel-and-disc mechanisms to perform the integration. In 1876, Sir William Thomson had already discussed the
possible construction of such calculators, but he had been stymied by the limited output torque of the ball-and-disk
integrators. In a differential analyzer, the output of one integrator drove the input of the next integrator, or a graphing
output. The torque amplifier was the advance that allowed these machines to work. Starting in the 1920s, <color=#3366CC>Vannevar</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bush</color> and others developed mechanical differential analyzers.
In the 1890s, the Spanish engineer Leonardo Torres Quevedo began to develop a series of advanced analog machines
that could solve real and complex roots of <color=#3366CC>polynomials</color>, which were published in 1901 by the Paris Academy of
Sciences.
First computer
<color=#3366CC>Charles Babbage</color>, an English mechanical engineer and <color=#3366CC>polymath</color>, originated the concept of a programmable computer.
Considered the "father of the computer", he conceptualized and invented the first mechanical computer in the early
19th century.
After working on his <color=#3366CC>difference engine</color> he announced his invention in 1822, in a paper to the Royal Astronomical
Society, titled "Note on the application of machinery to the computation of astronomical and mathematical tables". He
also designed to aid in navigational calculations, in 1833 he realized that a much more general design, an <color=#3366CC>analytical</color>
<color=#3366CC>engine</color>, was possible. The input of programs and data was to be provided to the machine via <color=#3366CC>punched cards</color>, a method
being used at the time to direct mechanical <color=#3366CC>looms</color> such as the <color=#3366CC>Jacquard loom</color>. For output, the machine would have a
<color=#3366CC>printer</color>, a curve plotter, and a bell. The machine would also be able to punch numbers onto cards to be read later. The
engine would incorporate an <color=#3366CC>arithmetic logic unit</color>, <color=#3366CC>control flow</color> in the form of conditional branching and <color=#3366CC>loops</color>, and
integrated <color=#3366CC>memory</color>, making it the first design for a general-purpose computer that could be described in modern terms
as Turing-complete.
The machine was about a century ahead of its time. All the parts for his machine had to be made by hand – this was a
major problem for a device with thousands of parts. Eventually, the project was dissolved with the decision of the <color=#3366CC>British</color>
<color=#3366CC>Government</color> to cease funding. Babbage's failure to complete the analytical engine can be chiefly attributed to political
and financial difficulties as well as his desire to develop an increasingly sophisticated computer and to move ahead
faster than anyone else could follow. Nevertheless, his son, Henry Babbage, completed a simplified version of the
analytical engine's computing unit (the mill) in 1888. He gave a successful demonstration of its use in computing tables
Electromechanical calculating machine
In his work Essays on Automatics published in 1914, Leonardo Torres Quevedo wrote a brief history of <color=#3366CC>Charles</color>
<color=#3366CC>Babbage</color>'s efforts at constructing a mechanical <color=#3366CC>Difference Engine</color> and <color=#3366CC>Analytical Engine</color>. The paper contains a design
of a machine capable of calculating formulas like, for a sequence of sets of values. The whole machine was to be
controlled by a <color=#3366CC>read-only</color> program, which was complete with provisions for conditional branching. He also introduced
the idea of <color=#3366CC>floating-point arithmetic</color>. In 1920, to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the invention of the arithmometer,
Torres presented in Paris the Electromechanical Arithmometer, which allowed a user to input arithmetic problems
through a keyboard, and computed and printed the results, demonstrating the feasibility of an electromechanical
analytical engine.
Analog computers
During the first half of the 20th century, many scientific <color=#3366CC>computing</color> needs were met by increasingly sophisticated analog
computers, which used a direct mechanical or electrical model of the problem as a basis for <color=#3366CC>computation</color>. However,
these were not programmable and generally lacked the versatility and accuracy of modern digital computers. The first
modern analog computer was a tide-predicting machine, invented by <color=#3366CC>Sir William Thomson</color> (later to become Lord
Kelvin) in 1872. The differential analyser, a mechanical analog computer designed to solve differential equations by
integration using wheel-and-disc mechanisms, was conceptualized in 1876 by James Thomson, the elder brother of the
more famous Sir William Thomson.
The art of mechanical analog computing reached its zenith with the differential analyzer, completed in 1931 by
<color=#3366CC>Vannevar Bush</color> at <color=#3366CC>MIT</color>. By the 1950s, the success of digital electronic computers had spelled the end for most analog
computing machines, but analog computers remained in use during the 1950s in some specialized applications such as
education (<color=#3366CC>slide rule</color>) and aircraft (control systems).
Digital computers
Electromechanical
<color=#3366CC>Claude Shannon</color>'s 1937 master's thesis laid the foundations of digital computing, with his insight of applying Boolean
algebra to the analysis and synthesis of switching circuits being the basic concept which underlies all electronic digital
computers.
By 1938, the United States Navy had developed the Torpedo Data Computer, an electromechanical analog computer
for <color=#3366CC>submarines</color> that used trigonometry to solve the problem of firing a torpedo at a moving target. During <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>,
similar devices were developed in other countries.
Early digital computers were electromechanical; electric switches drove mechanical relays to perform the calculation.
These devices had a low operating speed and were eventually superseded by much faster all-electric computers,
originally using <color=#3366CC>vacuum tubes</color>. The Z2, created by German engineer <color=#3366CC>Konrad Zuse</color> in 1939 in <color=#3366CC>Berlin</color>, was one of the
earliest examples of an electromechanical relay computer.
In 1941, Zuse followed his earlier machine with the <color=#3366CC>Z3</color>, the world's first working electromechanical <color=#3366CC>programmable</color>, fully
automatic digital computer. The Z3 was built with 2000 <color=#3366CC>relays</color>, implementing a 22-<color=#3366CC>bit</color> word length that operated at a
<color=#3366CC>clock frequency</color> of about 5–10 <color=#3366CC>Hz</color>. Program code was supplied on punched film while data could be stored in 64 words
of memory or supplied from the keyboard. It was quite similar to modern machines in some respects, pioneering
numerous advances such as <color=#3366CC>floating-point numbers</color>. Rather than the harder-to-implement decimal system (used in
<color=#3366CC>Charles Babbage</color>'s earlier design), using a <color=#3366CC>binary</color> system meant that Zuse's machines were easier to build and
potentially more reliable, given the technologies available at that time. The Z3 was not itself a universal computer but
could be extended to be Turing complete.
Zuse's next computer, the Z4, became the world's first commercial computer; after initial delay due to the Second World
War, it was completed in 1950 and delivered to the <color=#3366CC>ETH Zurich</color>. The computer was manufactured by Zuse's own
company, <color=#3366CC>Zuse KG</color>, which was founded in 1941 as the first company with the sole purpose of developing computers in
Berlin. The Z4 served as the inspiration for the construction of the ERMETH, the first Swiss computer and one of the
first in Europe.
Vacuum tubes and digital electronic circuits
Purely <color=#3366CC>electronic circuit</color> elements soon replaced their mechanical and electromechanical equivalents, at the same time
that digital calculation replaced analog. The engineer <color=#3366CC>Tommy Flowers</color>, working at the Post Office Research Station in
London in the 1930s, began to explore the possible use of electronics for the telephone exchange. Experimental
equipment that he built in 1934 went into operation five years later, converting a portion of the telephone exchange
network into an electronic data processing system, using thousands of <color=#3366CC>vacuum tubes</color>. In the US, <color=#3366CC>John Vincent</color>
<color=#3366CC>Atanasoff</color> and Clifford E. Berry of Iowa State University developed and tested the <color=#3366CC>Atanasoff–Berry Computer</color> (ABC) in
1942, the first "automatic electronic digital computer". This design was also all-electronic and used about 300 vacuum
tubes, with capacitors fixed in a mechanically rotating drum for memory.
During World War II, the British code-breakers at Bletchley Park achieved a number of successes in breaking
encrypted German military communications. The German encryption machine, <color=#3366CC>Enigma</color>, was first attacked with the help
of the electro-mechanical bombes which were often run by women. To crack the more sophisticated German Lorenz
SZ 40/42 machine, used for high-level Army communications, Max Newman and his colleagues commissioned Flowers
to build the <color=#3366CC>Colossus</color>. He spent eleven months from early February 1943 designing and building the first Colossus.
After a functional test in December 1943, Colossus was shipped to Bletchley Park, where it was delivered on 18
January 1944 and attacked its first message on 5 February.
Colossus was the world's first <color=#3366CC>electronic digital</color> programmable computer. It used a large number of valves (vacuum
tubes). It had paper-tape input and was capable of being configured to perform a variety of <color=#3366CC>boolean logic</color> algebraic
operations on its data, but it was not Turing-complete. Nine Mk II Colossi were built (The Mk I was converted to a Mk II,
making ten machines in total). Colossus Mark I contained 1,500 thermionic valves (tubes), but Mark II with 2,400
valves, was both five times faster and simpler to operate than Mark I, greatly speeding the decoding process.
The <color=#3366CC>ENIAC</color> (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was the first electronic <color=#3366CC>programmable</color> computer built in the
U.S. Although the ENIAC was similar to the Colossus, it was much faster, more flexible, and it was Turing-complete.
Like the Colossus, a "program" on the ENIAC was defined by the states of its patch cables and switches, a far cry from
the <color=#3366CC>stored program</color> electronic machines that came later. Once a program was written, it had to be mechanically set into
the machine with manual resetting of plugs and switches. The programmers of the ENIAC were six women, often
known collectively as the "ENIAC girls".
It combined the high speed of electronics with the ability to be programmed for many complex problems. It could add or
subtract 5000 times a second, a thousand times faster than any other machine. It also had modules to multiply, divide,
and take the square root. High-speed memory was limited to 20 words (about 80 bytes). Built under the direction of
John Mauchly and <color=#3366CC>J. Presper Eckert</color> at the University of Pennsylvania, ENIAC's development and construction lasted
from 1943 to full operation at the end of 1945. The machine was huge, weighing 30 tons, using 200 kilowatts of electric
power and contained over 18,000 vacuum tubes, 1,500 relays, and hundreds of thousands of resistors, capacitors, and
inductors.
Modern computers
Concept of modern computer
In his seminal 1936 paper, On Computable Numbers, <color=#3366CC>Alan Turing</color> proposed the principle of the modern computer.
Turing proposed a simple device that he called "Universal Computing machine" and that is now known as a <color=#3366CC>universal</color>
<color=#3366CC>Turing machine</color>. He proved that such a machine is capable of computing anything that is computable by executing
instructions (program) stored on tape, allowing the machine to be programmable. The fundamental concept of Turing's
design is the <color=#3366CC>stored program</color>, where all the instructions for computing are stored in memory. <color=#3366CC>Von Neumann</color>
acknowledged that the central concept of the modern computer was due to this paper. Turing machines are to this day
a central object of study in <color=#3366CC>theory of computation</color>. Except for the limitations imposed by their finite memory stores,
modern computers are said to be Turing-complete, which is to say, they have <color=#3366CC>algorithm</color> execution capability equivalent
to a universal Turing machine.
Stored programs
Early computing machines had fixed programs. Changing their function required the re-wiring and re-structuring of the
machine. With the proposal of the stored-program computer this changed. A stored-program computer includes by
design an <color=#3366CC>instruction set</color> and can store in memory a set of instructions (a <color=#3366CC>program</color>) that details the <color=#3366CC>computation</color>. The
theoretical basis for the stored-program computer was laid out by Turing in his 1936 paper. In 1945, Turing joined the
National Physical Laboratory and began work on developing an electronic stored-program digital computer. His 1945
report "Proposed Electronic Calculator" was the first specification for such a device. John von Neumann at the
<color=#3366CC>University of Pennsylvania</color> also circulated his First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC in 1945.
The Manchester Baby was the world's first <color=#3366CC>stored-program computer</color>. It was built at the <color=#3366CC>University of Manchester</color> in
England by Frederic C. Williams, Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill, and ran its first program on 21 June 1948. It was
designed as a testbed for the Williams tube, the first <color=#3366CC>random-access</color> digital storage device. Although the computer was
described as "small and primitive" by a 1998 retrospective, it was the first working machine to contain all of the
elements essential to a modern electronic computer. As soon as the Baby had demonstrated the feasibility of its
design, a project began at the university to develop it into a practically useful computer, the Manchester Mark 1.
The Mark 1 in turn quickly became the prototype for the Ferranti Mark 1, the world's first commercially available
general-purpose computer. Built by Ferranti, it was delivered to the University of Manchester in February 1951. At least
seven of these later machines were delivered between 1953 and 1957, one of them to <color=#3366CC>Shell</color> labs in <color=#3366CC>Amsterdam</color>. In
October 1947 the directors of British catering company J. Lyons & Company decided to take an active role in promoting
the commercial development of computers. Lyons's LEO I computer, modelled closely on the Cambridge <color=#3366CC>EDSAC</color> of
1949, became operational in April 1951 and ran the world's first routine office computer job. Meanwhile, in 1950,
independent of Western projects and working in post-WWII war-torn Kyiv, a team led by Sergey Lebedev at the Kyiv
Institute of Electrotechnology developed the MESM (Small Electronic Calculating Machine). It became the first
operational programmable electronic computer in continental Europe, featuring an advanced internal random-access
memory architecture based entirely on electronic vacuum-tube flip-flops (triggers) for immediate data processing,
supplemented by a magnetic drum for secondary storage.
Transistors
The concept of a <color=#3366CC>field-effect transistor</color> was proposed by Julius Edgar Lilienfeld in 1925. <color=#3366CC>John Bardeen</color> and <color=#3366CC>Walter</color>

<color=#3366CC>Brattain</color>, while working under <color=#3366CC>William Shockley</color> at <color=#3366CC>Bell Labs</color>, built the first working <color=#3366CC>transistor</color>, the point-contact transistor,
in 1947, which was followed by Shockley's <color=#3366CC>bipolar junction transistor</color> in 1948. From 1955 onwards, transistors replaced
<color=#3366CC>vacuum tubes</color> in computer designs, giving rise to the "second generation" of computers. Compared to vacuum tubes,
transistors have many advantages: they are smaller, and require less power than vacuum tubes, so give off less heat.
<color=#3366CC>Junction transistors</color> were much more reliable than vacuum tubes and had longer, indefinite, service life. Transistorized
computers could contain tens of thousands of binary logic circuits in a relatively compact space. However, early
junction transistors were relatively bulky devices that were difficult to manufacture on a <color=#3366CC>mass-production</color> basis, which
limited them to a number of specialized applications.
At the <color=#3366CC>University of Manchester</color>, a team under the leadership of Tom Kilburn designed and built a machine using the
newly developed transistors instead of valves. Their first transistorized computer and the first in the world, was
<color=#3366CC>operational by 1953</color>, and a second version was completed there in April 1955. However, the machine did make use of
valves to generate its 125 kHz clock waveforms and in the circuitry to read and write on its magnetic drum memory, so
it was not the first completely transistorized computer. That distinction goes to the Harwell CADET of 1955, built by the
electronics division of the Atomic Energy Research Establishment at Harwell.
The <color=#3366CC>metal–oxide–silicon field-effect transistor</color> (MOSFET), also known as the MOS transistor, was invented at Bell Labs
between 1955 and 1960 and was the first truly compact transistor that could be miniaturized and mass-produced for a
wide range of uses. With its <color=#3366CC>high scalability</color>, and much lower power consumption and higher density than bipolar
junction transistors, the MOSFET made it possible to build <color=#3366CC>high-density integrated circuits</color>. In addition to data
processing, it also enabled the practical use of MOS transistors as memory cell storage elements, leading to the
development of MOS semiconductor memory, which replaced earlier magnetic-core memory in computers. The
MOSFET led to the microcomputer revolution, and became the driving force behind the <color=#3366CC>computer revolution</color>. The
MOSFET is the most widely used transistor in computers, and is the fundamental building block of <color=#3366CC>digital electronics</color>.
Integrated circuits
The next great advance in computing power came with the advent of the <color=#3366CC>integrated circuit</color> (IC). The idea of the
integrated circuit was first conceived by a radar scientist working for the Royal Radar Establishment of the Ministry of
Defence, Geoffrey W.A. Dummer. Dummer presented the first public description of an integrated circuit at the
Symposium on Progress in Quality Electronic Components in <color=#3366CC>Washington, D.C.</color>, on 7 May 1952.
The first working ICs were invented by <color=#3366CC>Jack Kilby</color> at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor.
Kilby recorded his initial ideas concerning the integrated circuit in July 1958, successfully demonstrating the first
working integrated example on 12 September 1958. In his patent application of 6 February 1959, Kilby described his
new device as "a body of semiconductor material ... wherein all the components of the electronic circuit are completely
integrated". However, Kilby's invention was a hybrid integrated circuit (hybrid IC), rather than a <color=#3366CC>monolithic integrated</color>
<color=#3366CC>circuit</color> (IC) chip. Kilby's IC had external wire connections, which made it difficult to mass-produce.
Noyce also came up with his own idea of an integrated circuit half a year later than Kilby. Noyce's invention was the
first true monolithic IC chip, and solved many practical problems that Kilby's had not. Produced at Fairchild
Semiconductor, it was made of <color=#3366CC>silicon</color>, whereas Kilby's chip was made of <color=#3366CC>germanium</color>. Noyce's monolithic IC was
fabricated using the planar process, developed by his colleague Jean Hoerni in early 1959. In turn, the planar process
was based on Carl Frosch and Lincoln Derick work on semiconductor surface passivation by silicon dioxide.
Modern monolithic ICs are predominantly MOS (<color=#3366CC>metal–oxide–semiconductor</color>) integrated circuits, built from <color=#3366CC>MOSFETs</color>
(MOS transistors). The earliest experimental MOS IC to be fabricated was a 16-transistor chip built by Fred Heiman
and Steven Hofstein at RCA in 1962. General Microelectronics later introduced the first commercial MOS IC in 1964,
developed by Robert Norman. Following the development of the self-aligned gate (silicon-gate) MOS transistor by
Robert Kerwin, Donald Klein and John Sarace at Bell Labs in 1967, the first silicon-gate MOS IC with self-aligned gates
was developed by Federico Faggin at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1968. The MOSFET has since become the most
critical device component in modern ICs.
The development of the MOS integrated circuit led to the invention of the <color=#3366CC>microprocessor</color>, and heralded an explosion in
the commercial and personal use of computers. While the subject of exactly which device was the first microprocessor
is contentious, partly due to lack of agreement on the exact definition of the term "microprocessor", it is largely
undisputed that the first single-chip microprocessor was the Intel 4004, designed and realized by Federico Faggin with
his silicon-gate MOS IC technology, along with Ted Hoff, Masatoshi Shima and Stanley Mazor at <color=#3366CC>Intel</color>. In the early
1970s, MOS IC technology enabled the <color=#3366CC>integration</color> of more than 10,000 transistors on a single chip.
<color=#3366CC>System on a Chip</color> (SoCs) are complete computers on a <color=#3366CC>microchip</color> (or chip) the size of a coin. They may or may not
have integrated <color=#3366CC>RAM</color> and <color=#3366CC>flash memory</color>. If not integrated, the RAM is usually placed directly above (known as Package
on package) or below (on the opposite side of the <color=#3366CC>circuit board</color>) the SoC, and the flash memory is usually placed right
next to the SoC. This is done to improve data transfer speeds, as the data signals do not have to travel long distances.
Since ENIAC in 1945, computers have advanced enormously, with modern SoCs (such as the Snapdragon 865) being
the size of a coin while also being hundreds of thousands of times more powerful than ENIAC, integrating billions of
transistors, and consuming only a few watts of power.
Mobile computers
The first mobile computers were heavy and ran from mains power. The 50 lb IBM 5100 was an early example. Later
portables such as the Osborne 1 and Compaq Portable were considerably lighter but still needed to be plugged in. The
first laptops, such as the Grid Compass, removed this requirement by incorporating batteries – and with the continued
miniaturization of computing resources and advancements in portable battery life, portable computers grew in
popularity in the 2000s. The same developments allowed manufacturers to integrate computing resources into cellular
mobile phones by the early 2000s.
These <color=#3366CC>smartphones</color> and <color=#3366CC>tablets</color> run on a variety of operating systems and recently became the dominant computing
device on the market. These are powered by <color=#3366CC>System on a Chip</color> (SoCs), which are complete computers on a microchip
the size of a coin.

Unconventional computers

A computer does not need to be <color=#3366CC>electronic</color>, nor even have a <color=#3366CC>processor</color>, nor <color=#3366CC>RAM</color>, nor even a <color=#3366CC>hard disk</color>. While popular
usage of the word "computer" is synonymous with a personal electronic computer, a typical modern definition of a
computer is: "A device that computes, especially a programmable [usually] electronic machine that performs
high-speed mathematical or logical operations or that assembles, stores, correlates, or otherwise processes
information." According to this definition, any device that processes information qualifies as a computer.
Hardware
The term hardware covers all tangible physical parts of a computer. Circuits, <color=#3366CC>computer chips</color>, <color=#3366CC>graphics cards</color>, <color=#3366CC>sound</color>

<color=#3366CC>cards</color>, <color=#3366CC>memory (RAM)</color>, <color=#3366CC>motherboards</color>, <color=#3366CC>displays</color>, power supplies, cables, <color=#3366CC>keyboards</color>, <color=#3366CC>printers</color> and <color=#3366CC>computer mice</color> are all
hardware.
History of computing hardware
Other hardware topics
A general-purpose computer has four main components: the <color=#3366CC>arithmetic logic unit</color> (ALU), the control unit, the <color=#3366CC>memory</color>,
and the <color=#3366CC>input and output devices</color> (collectively termed I/O). These parts are interconnected by <color=#3366CC>buses</color>, often made of
groups of wires. Inside each of these parts are thousands to trillions of small electrical circuits which can be turned off
or on by means of an electronic switch. Each circuit represents a <color=#3366CC>bit</color> (binary digit) of information so that when the circuit
is on it represents a "1", and when off it represents a "0" (in positive logic representation). The circuits are arranged in
<color=#3366CC>logic gates</color> so that one or more of the circuits may control the state of one or more of the other circuits.
Input devices
<color=#3366CC>Input devices</color> are the means by which the operations of a computer are controlled and it is provided with data.
Examples include:
• <color=#3366CC>Computer keyboard</color>
• Digital camera
• Graphics tablet
• <color=#3366CC>Image scanner</color>
• Joystick
• <color=#3366CC>Microphone</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Mouse</color>
